PCP.Algebraic.BinaryLocalCorrection.fail.text: Fix a target $a$ and a polynomial $P$ of degree at most $D\ge cb^c$. Assume $q>2c$, the stated interpolation nodes and homogeneous distance at most $\delta$ between the points table and the affine encoding of $P$; the lines table can be arbitrary. The failure event includes both rejection and returning a wrong bit. Its probability is at most $C\kappa_a+\delta+D/[2(q-1)]$, averaging all randomness, including the homogeneous label. The estimate applies separately at every target, without a uniform bound on $\kappa_a$.

PCP.Algebraic.BinaryLocalCorrection.soun.text: The constant in the local-correction estimate is $C=2+2(c+1)K$. The two terms involving $K$ account for replacing the corrected answers at the sampled point and at the target by their decoded polynomial values. The remaining two units multiply rejection losses. The formula depends only on the fixed inner degree $c$, not on the target, graph size, outer dimension or received proof.

PCP.Algebraic.BinaryLocalRowDecoding.dec.text: The inner decoding constant is $K=4(c+2)^2(112(c+2)+60)$. It gives a single bound valid at every rejection probability for both full-label and homogeneous distances. Its size accommodates the transition from the small-error low-degree theorem to the trivial distance bound of one. It is a sufficient uniform constant; the formal definition does not assert that it is optimal.

PCP.Algebraic.BinaryLocalRowDecoding.exi.text: Assume characteristic two, a binary coordinate isomorphism, label degree $r\ge1$, generator-based interpolation nodes and $q>2c$. Every received table has one degree-at-most-$c$ polynomial whose encoding is within $K\kappa$ on both the full-label and homogeneous-label distributions. Here $\kappa$ is the rejection probability of the fair mixture defining the inner test. There is no small-rejection premise: when the estimate exceeds one, the universal distance bound suffices.

PCP.Algebraic.BinaryZeroOnGridCorrection.text: For a nonempty grid, let $A$ and $M$ have degrees at most $D\ge cb^c$, and assume $q>2c$ and the stated interpolation nodes. The points tables need only be globally close on homogeneous labels, with errors $\delta_A$ and $\delta_M$; the certificate’s lines table remains arbitrary. If $A$ is nonzero somewhere on the grid, the formal statement gives (15). Each corrector’s rejection is averaged over the targets requested by the test, not bounded separately at every target.

PCP.Algebraic.DerivedZeroOnGrid.TestSamp.text: The test samples an outer point, a homogeneous label shared by the two certificate requests, independent randomness for those two local-corrector calls, and a fresh uniform label from $\mathcal B_r$ for the primary self-corrected read. The last label supplies the randomness in (9). Independence of that fresh choice is what permits the $2\epsilon$ replacement estimate even when the requested primary label depends on the point and the homogeneous label.

PCP.Algebraic.DerivedZeroOnGrid.rejectio.text: Assume $b\ge1$, $q>2c$, generator test nodes and distinct nonzero correction nodes. At each point $x$, let $A_x$ have degree at most $r$, and assume the function $x\mapsto A_x(g(x))$ is represented by a polynomial $A$ of degree at most $D\ge cb^c$. Let the certificate polynomial $M$ also have degree at most $D$, with homogeneous table error $\delta_M$, and suppose $A$ does not vanish on the nonempty grid. The primary full-label error $\epsilon$ contributes $2\epsilon$ to rejection before the grid estimate, so it is multiplied by $1+2C$ in (16).

PCP.Algebraic.EncodedLineLowDegreeTest.A.text: A lines table assigns a binary function to every ordered pair consisting of a base point and a slope. Each function is indexed by an inner point in $F^{cb}$ and an affine label in $\mathcal B_1$. This applies even when the associated points table uses cubic labels. Arbitrary received entries need not represent polynomials and need not agree when two indices describe the same geometric line.

PCP.Algebraic.EncodedLineLowDegreeTest.e.text: The input is an arbitrary points table and an arbitrary lines table; no agreement among line indices is assumed. With positive base $b$, degree bound $D=cb^c$, label degree $r\ge1$, the stated interpolation nodes, $q\ge10^6D^3$ and $J\kappa\le1/(4\cdot10^6)$, the formal statement produces one polynomial of degree at most $D$. Its encoding satisfies both full-label and homogeneous error bounds $S\kappa$. The homogeneous estimate concerns linear labels with zero constant term.

PCP.Algebraic.EncodedLineLowDegreeTest.l.text: The field-valued point-versus-line disagreement is bounded by $J\kappa$, where $J=2((c+1)K+29)$. The correction replacement contributes $(c+1)K$, the tested comparison contributes one and decoding the points table contributes $28$. Passing from the disagreement of homogeneous observations to field-valued disagreement contributes the factor two. This is the error budget to which the point-versus-line threshold is applied.

PCP.Algebraic.EncodedLineLowDegreeTest.s.text: The final distance factor is $S=28+J$, with $J$ defined by the preceding line-disagreement estimate. The point-versus-line theorem gives field distance at most $2J\kappa$; encoding halves that contribution, and the original points-table decoding contributes at most $28\kappa$. Both full-label and homogeneous distances are bounded by $S\kappa$ for the same polynomial, which lets subsequent tests use a single fixed choice.

PCP.Algebraic.GeneratorLowDegreeTest.exi.text: Let $F$ be any finite field with $q>2c$, and use the first $c+1$ nonzero powers of a generator of $F^\times$, with their Lagrange weights at zero. If the weighted test rejects with probability at most $\delta<1/[2(c+2)^2]$, some polynomial of total degree at most $c$ is within distance $2\delta$ of the received function. The claim is existential and imposes no computational requirement on finding that polynomial.

PCP.Algebraic.GridVanishing.IsCertificat.text: A vanishing certificate satisfies the two polynomial identities $M(X,0)=0$ and $M(X,Z_H(X))=A(X)$. These are equalities of polynomials, not merely agreement of their evaluations on field points. The definition contains no degree restriction and does not require $M$ to be linear in its second block. Degree bounds are hypotheses or conclusions of the separate certificate theorems.

PCP.Algebraic.GridVanishing.vanishesOn_i.text: Let $H$ be a nonempty finite subset of an integral domain and use finitely many variables. The formal statement equates vanishing of $A$ on $H^k$ with existence of a polynomial $M(X,Y)$ of total degree at most $\deg A$ satisfying the polynomial identities $M(X,0)=0$ and $M(X,Z_H(X))=A(X)$. The identities impose no linearity requirement on $M$ in $Y$. Nonemptiness is needed for the degree-preserving certificate construction.

PCP.Algebraic.PointLineTest.exists_close.text: Over any finite field, let each ordered base-point and slope pair have an arbitrary univariate polynomial of degree at most $D$. If its disagreement probability with the points function is $\theta\le1/(4\cdot10^6)$ and $q\ge10^6D^3$, the formal statement gives a multivariate polynomial of total degree at most $D$ at distance at most $2\theta$. Parameters range over all of $F$, zero slopes are allowed, and the conclusion also covers $D=0$ and dimension zero.

PCP.Algebraic.SetMultilinear.eval_encode.text: For a univariate polynomial $T$ of degree below $b^c$, substituting the point $\Phi(z)_{i,s}=z^{s b^i}$ into its set-multilinear encoding recovers $T(z)$ exactly. The degree hypothesis is strict. This is the identity used for honest line restrictions; it does not say that every polynomial of total degree at most $c$ in the inner variables is the encoding of an honest low-degree line polynomial.

PCP.Algebraic.ThreeColorAmplifiedVerifie.text: For the particular positive repetition count $R$ chosen by the construction, the formal statement combines all probability and resource guarantees of the amplified graph verifier: at most $187R$ queries, exactly $32000000R(\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil+1)$ random bits, polynomially bounded proof addresses, perfect completeness and soundness error at most $1/2$. It concerns three-colourability of the graph decoded from the input. Polynomial running time and the reduction from an arbitrary NP language are established separately.

PCP.Algebraic.ThreeColorGrid.colorable_i.text: The formal statement concerns existence: a graph on $H^m$ is three-colourable exactly when there exists a polynomial $P$ of degree at most $d_0=m(h-1)$ whose vertex and edge constraints vanish on their grids. It assumes characteristic two and a primitive cube root of unity. The fixed-$P$ characterization and the separate bounds $d_0,3d_0,5d_0$ require the neighbouring constraint and degree results; they are not conclusions of this one statement.

PCP.Algebraic.ThreeColorGrid.constraints.text: For a fixed polynomial $P$, the formal statement equates vanishing of $P^3-1$ on $H^m$ and of $E(X,Y)(P(X)-P(Y))^3-E(X,Y)$ on $H^{2m}$ with the corresponding vertex and edge equations for its grid values. It imposes no degree bound. The separate facts about cube roots turn these equations into a proper three-colouring in characteristic two.

PCP.Algebraic.ThreeColorVerifier.Proof.text: Four points tables carry the colouring, its difference and the two vanishing certificates. Their domains are $F^m,F^{2m},F^{2m},F^{4m}$, with cubic labels for the first two polynomial roles and affine labels for the certificates. Each has one associated encoded lines table. The definition places no honesty or consistency requirement on received bits. The same certificate lines table is used by its low-degree test and by later local-correction calls.

PCP.Algebraic.ThreeColorVerifier.Query.text: A full proof address selects one of eight tables. A points-table address then supplies an outer point and a label; a lines-table address supplies the line’s base point and slope, an inner point and an affine label. The allowed label degree is three for colouring and difference points, and one for all certificate points and lines tables. This specifies locations only; honest values require the separate encoding construction.

PCP.Algebraic.ThreeColorVerifier.Sample.text: A full graph-verifier seed supplies a separate seed for each of the seven checks. These are four binary low-degree tests, two zero-on-grid tests using self-corrected primary reads, and the difference-consistency check. Uniform sampling from the product makes the check seeds independent. The verifier accepts only when all checks accept; no random choice selects just one of the seven checks.

PCP.Algebraic.ThreeColorVerifier.exists_.text: The formal statement starts with a three-colourable graph on a nonempty grid and assumes $5m(h-1)<b^c$, characteristic two, the binary coordinates, a primitive cube root and suitable interpolation nodes. It constructs one eight-table proof accepted for every seed. The degree condition is a sufficient bound for the colouring extension and both certificates. When the polynomials and certificates are already supplied with their actual degrees below $b^c$, the direct perfect-completeness statement applies under that more specific information.

PCP.Algebraic.ThreeColorVerifier.properA.text: The edge-certificate corrector uses the same received lines table that accompanies the edge-certificate points table in its low-degree test. Its targets have two blocks of $2m$ coordinates after the pair of vertex-coordinate blocks is placed in one list. This is only a change of coordinate indexing; no additional proof entries are introduced, and the table remains arbitrary in the soundness analysis.

PCP.Algebraic.ThreeColorVerifier.read.text: The formal definition reads one bit from the table selected by a full address. It accepts arbitrary received tables and does not impose polynomiality or agreement between them. For an honest proof, the encoding construction supplies the value $R(\rho(u))$ at a points-table address, so the read operation returns that value. Keeping this distinction explicit matters in soundness, where the verifier must also operate on inconsistent proofs.

PCP.Algebraic.ThreeColorVerifier.validAu.text: The vertex-certificate corrector uses exactly the lines table paired with the vertex-certificate points table in its binary low-degree test. At a prescribed target, it selects an entry by that target and the sampled slope. This reuse keeps the proof to eight tables. Each correction call still tests its selected entry, and the generic correction estimate permits arbitrary received lines tables while accounting for that call’s own rejection probability.

PCP.InNP.text: Membership means that there exists a polynomial witness bound and a witness-checking relation satisfying the chosen notion of polynomial time. This definition alone does not select a machine model. In the forward and reverse PCP theorems, the notion is fixed to concrete finite-machine polynomial time, and the reference-NP equivalence identifies that resulting class with the reference nondeterministic-machine class.

PCP.Lang.ThreeColorRuntime.polyTimeAlg.text: The formal statement certifies polynomial running time for the concrete step algorithm of the amplified three-colourability verifier, measured by a finite multi-stack machine. Its proof combines a program-cost bound with the implementation of amplification. This is the runtime fact used when assembling the final PCP theorem. The details of finding a finite field and roots, and translating the program into machine steps, lie in imported constructions that are not all included in this packet.

PCP.Machine.PolyTimeAlg.text: Polynomial time is measured for one verifier step as a function of the total encoded length of the input, random string and proof answers received so far. A step either returns a final Boolean decision or the next natural-number proof address. The formal definition requires an actual finite multi-stack machine computing this operation within a polynomial number of steps, rather than treating field arithmetic or table indexing as unit-cost black boxes.

PCP.NPCertificate.text: The definition supplies a Boolean relation $\mathcal R$ and polynomial $p_{\rm w}$ with $x\in\mathcal L$ exactly when some $w$ of length at most $p_{\rm w}(|x|)$ satisfies $\mathcal R(x,w)=1$. Polynomial-time checkability is a parameter of this definition. The forward theorem supplies the concrete machine notion of polynomial time; it does not prove the PCP theorem for an arbitrary choice of what counts as an efficient relation.

PCP.QueryTree.text: A decision tree has an upper bound on the number of proof bits read along a branch. Each internal node names a natural-number address and branches on its Boolean answer; a leaf accepts or rejects. Leaves may occur before the bound is exhausted. Consequently the fixed query parameter is a worst-case upper bound, not a requirement that every run performs exactly that many reads.

PCP.ReferenceNP.inNP_iff_mem.text: The formal statement identifies two classes of binary languages: those with polynomially bounded witnesses checked in polynomial time by the concrete machine model, and the reference class defined by nondeterministic machines. It proves both implications for every language. Thus the NP hypothesis and conclusion in Theorem 1.1 can be read in the reference sense. The equality is a mathematical theorem; the separate claim that a vendored source tree is unchanged requires repository provenance.

PCP.Verifier.ImplementedBy.text: The formal condition identifies the verifier’s tree with the algorithm expanded only up to the allowed query depth. It compares every input, seed and possible answer branch. At depth zero, a further query request is converted into rejection, so the condition does not require the algorithm itself to halt within the query budget. A separate polynomial-time condition bounds the machine computation of each step. Together they give the implemented bounded verifier used in Theorem 1.1.

PCP.Verifier.ReadsBelow.text: The proof-address bound quantifies over every seed and every address occurring on any branch of the selected query tree. Thus it is independent of the proof’s answers. Taking the bound to be $p(n)$ means that only the first $p(n)$ bits of an infinite proof oracle can matter. This is the formal form of polynomial proof length used in both directions of Theorem 1.1.

PCP.np_subset_pcp.text: For each NP language, the formal statement chooses one verifier and one polynomial-time implementation. On every input of length $n$, it uses exactly $\alpha\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil+\beta$ fair bits, asks at most a fixed $\ell$ proof-bit queries and reads only addresses below $p(n)$. The implementation, constants and polynomial are fixed before the input. Completeness chooses one proof before the random seed; soundness bounds every fixed proof’s acceptance probability by $1/2$.

PCP.pcp_subset_np_concrete.text: Suppose one verifier has a polynomial-time implementation, the exact randomness budget $\alpha\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil+\beta$, a polynomial bound on all proof addresses, perfect completeness and soundness error at most $1/2$. The formal statement concludes that its language has a concrete polynomial-time witness checker with polynomially bounded witnesses. The machine model is fixed. The paper’s witness is the accessible proof prefix, and logarithmic randomness makes exhaustive seed enumeration polynomial in the input length.
